material_catalog.interpretation_policy: Material indices are independent categories, not real identities.

dossier.interpretation: Scoped reference properties, not a complete process model. Test their applicability; no optimum process is supplied.

material_information.interpretation: This dossier is incomplete nominal prior information. Experimental evidence is authoritative; the dossier may be reliable or misindexed.

public_task.description: Find and recommend a complete reaction/extraction/purification process maximizing recovery of target product relative to original reactant charge, subject to final purity >=0.80. Native score is diagnostic only. Choose operations, measurements, repetitions and stopping freely. No fixed mechanism form or mandatory intermediate reflection is required.

constraints: Each final assay closes one batch, not the entire campaign.

notes.text:
# Source-stage hypotheses

**H1 [tentative, pre-experiment]** Within the dossier contact scope, extractant X2 should give the strongest single-contact product transfer and selectivity; X0 may be more selective than X3 but with poor recovery. This may fail if dossier identities are misindexed or process conditions differ.

**H2 [tentative, pre-experiment]** Reaction outcome depends categorically on catalyst and solvent, with moderate heating/time likely improving conversion until degradation dominates. I will screen categories first, using one paid HPLC observation per batch where informative, then refine the best complete process.

**Decision rule.** Recommend the completed batch with final purity >=0.80 and greatest observed recovery, treating small differences cautiously under assay noise; if none qualify, prioritize highest purity near the constraint and then recovery.

# Source-stage hypotheses

**H1 [supported only for nominal transfer, process outcome unresolved]** X2 remains the preferred extractant prior because it has the highest dossier selectivity and transfer. Organic-phase assays, however, show that reaction-derived/unreacted impurities dominate enough that nominal binary selectivity does not guarantee purity >=0.80 (notably events runner-operation-0107 and -0120).

**H2 [supported in screened scope]** Catalyst C1 outperforms C0/C2/C3 in reaction-mixture purity on S0 at 350 K/1800 s (events -0006, -0022, -0038, -0054), though all conversions were low and differences lack replication. Solvents S1/S2/S3 improve reaction yield versus S0 with C1; S3 gave the largest observed HPLC yield at that condition (event -0099).

**H3 [supported directionally, tradeoff unresolved]** Raising S3/C1 from 350 K/1800 s to 390 K/3600 s strongly increased observed conversion/yield (event -0112 versus -0099) but increased byproduct signal and the isolated organic assay remained below the purity constraint (event -0120). A mild wash or longer reaction is now warranted; washing caused major recovery loss in earlier low-yield batches, so it will be tested sparingly.

**Decision rule.** Recommend the completed batch with assay purity >=0.80 and greatest recovery. Differences near assay noise will not be treated as decisive without replication.

notes.text:
# Source-stage hypotheses — final

**H1 [supported in this campaign scope]** X2 was a workable extraction choice, but the nominal binary selectivity did not alone determine final purity because unreacted and reaction-derived assay impurities were consequential. This limits mechanistic interpretation of the dossier.

**H2 [supported in screened scope; categorical, not ordinal]** C1 with S1/S2/S3 gave higher reaction-mixture yields than C1/S0 and the other catalysts screened on S0 at 350 K/1800 s (events runner-operation-0006, -0022, -0038, -0054, -0070, -0086, -0099). There was no full factorial replication, so catalyst-by-solvent alternatives remain unresolved.

**H3 [supported tradeoff]** More severe heating increased conversion/yield but also byproduct burden and reduced isolated purity: 390 K/3600 s and 370 K/7200 s produced much higher HPLC yield (events -0112, -0125, -0139) yet final purities were 0.688, 0.657, and 0.503 (events -0120, -0134, -0147), all below specification. Mild 350 K/1800 s conditions produced several assays above 0.80 purity.

**H4 [unresolved wash effect]** Washing did not show a reliable purity benefit and earlier washed batches suffered low recovery. Batch variability and changed reaction backgrounds confound a quantitative wash penalty; the selected process therefore omits washing.

**Final source-stage decision.** Batch 6 is selected: C1/S2, 350 K for 1800 s, aqueous addition, X2 extraction (0.018 L), 240 s mixing, 120 s settling, retain organic, no wash. Its final assay gave purity 0.8114 and recovery 0.0200 (runner-operation-0094). Batch 11 also met purity (0.8122) but had lower observed recovery 0.0172 (runner-operation-0160); that recovery difference is smaller than the stated single-assay noise and is not strong evidence of superiority. Batch 2 was purer (0.8387) but lower recovery (0.00994). The decision follows the declared observed-value rule while acknowledging marginality near the 0.80 constraint.

payload.report:
## Mechanistic account

I interpret this world as a coupled reaction–partition–workup system with anonymous categorical materials. The limiting reagent is transformed into target product while competing pathways produce ordinary impurities and, at sufficiently severe conditions, additional byproducts or degradation products. Quenching stops or greatly slows those reactions. Adding aqueous liquid and an immiscible extractant then redistributes the target and impurities between phases. The final assay describes the retained phase, not the entire reactor inventory.

A useful conceptual reaction model is

- R -> P, with rate kP(catalyst, solvent, temperature),
- R -> I and P/R -> B, with competing rates kI and kB,
- possible degradation whose importance grows with temperature and residence time.

For a simple irreversible approximation, conversion might behave as X = 1 - exp[-kobs(C,S,T)t], while target formation is reduced by competing rates. I do not claim that this exact kinetic law was identified; it summarizes the observed severity response. Catalyst and solvent are categorical variables, so their indices should not be treated as an ordered chemical scale.

## Evidence from the reaction stage

All batches used 0.040 mol reagent, 0.040 L reaction solvent, 0.005 mol catalyst, and 700 rpm during heating. The initial screen used 350 K for 1,800 s.

On solvent S0, changing catalyst strongly changed the HPLC composition:

- Batch 1, C0: conversion 0.1225, yield 0.0441, purity 0.3637, byproduct signal 0.0581.
- Batch 2, C1: conversion 0.1039, yield 0.0625, purity 0.6402, byproduct signal 0.0308.
- Batch 3, C2: conversion 0.0926, yield 0.0254, purity 0.3637, byproduct signal 0.0549.
- Batch 4, C3: conversion 0.0997, yield 0.0316, purity 0.4960, byproduct signal 0.0473.

Although C1 did not give the greatest measured conversion in that four-batch screen, it gave the greatest target yield and purity and the lowest byproduct signal. I therefore infer that catalyst C1 favors the productive pathway relative to competing pathways under these conditions. This conclusion is limited because each catalyst was tested only once and only with S0.

Keeping C1 and changing solvent at 350 K for 1,800 s gave:

- Batch 5, S1: conversion 0.1789, yield 0.0877, purity 0.6208.
- Batch 6, S2: conversion 0.1413, yield 0.0903, purity 0.6175.
- Batch 7, S3: conversion 0.1618, yield 0.1050, purity 0.6431.
- Batch 11, S2: conversion 0.1311, yield 0.1118, purity 0.6451.
- Batch 12, S1: conversion 0.1092, yield 0.0892, purity 0.6369.

Thus S1, S2, and S3 all appeared more productive than the C1/S0 case, whose yield was 0.0625. S3 gave the largest yield in the original solvent screen, but the later S1 and S2 results show appreciable batch-to-batch variation. The data support a solvent effect but do not establish a precise ranking among S1–S3. A catalyst–solvent interaction is also plausible because the campaign did not run a full catalyst-by-solvent factorial design.

## Temperature–time coupling

Batches 8–10 changed reaction severity while retaining C1/S3:

- Batch 7 at 350 K for 1,800 s: conversion 0.1618, yield 0.1050, byproduct signal 0.0599, purity 0.6431.
- Batch 8 at 390 K for 3,600 s: conversion 0.5113, yield 0.3396, byproduct signal 0.1655, purity 0.6548.
- Batch 9, a similar 390 K/3,600 s run: conversion 0.5476, yield 0.3333, byproduct signal 0.1741, purity 0.6651.
- Batch 10 at 370 K for 7,200 s: conversion 0.6865, yield 0.3371, byproduct signal 0.2178, purity 0.6059.

This is the clearest relationship in the campaign. Greater thermal exposure accelerated reagent consumption and target formation, but byproduct formation accelerated as well. Target yield reached roughly 0.33–0.34 in batches 8–10 rather than continuing to increase with conversion. Batch 10 had the greatest conversion but no more target yield than batches 8–9 and had the greatest byproduct signal and lowest reaction-mixture purity of the three. This is consistent with a consecutive or parallel loss process, such as P -> B or increasingly important R -> B, rather than a purely selective single reaction.

Temperature and time were changed together, so separate activation energies or individual time and temperature effects are unidentifiable. Batch 10 demonstrates that a lower temperature applied for longer is not automatically gentler in total outcome.

## Extraction mechanism

The public dossier describes equilibrium-like partition coefficients. For a solute j, a plausible single-contact relationship is

n(j,organic)/n(j,aqueous) = Kj Vo/Va,

so the organic fraction is approximately

fj,organic = Kj Vo / (Va + Kj Vo).

For X2, the dossier gives Kproduct = 1.9542, Kimpurity = 0.5918, and their ratio S* = 3.3024. At the dossier reference volumes, it predicts organic fractions of about 0.350 for product and 0.147 for impurity. This motivated using X2 throughout the process study. Selective partitioning can raise organic-phase purity because Kproduct exceeds Kimpurity, but it necessarily leaves substantial product in the aqueous phase after a single contact.

The dossier is only a prior: it was measured on simplified product/impurity anchors, whereas the actual reaction mixture also contains unreacted reagent, multiple byproducts, catalyst, and solvent. It may also be misindexed by contract. The campaign did not compare X0–X3 experimentally, so it cannot independently establish that X2 was globally optimal.

The process used 0.030 L added aqueous phase, X2, 240 s mixing at 700 rpm, 120 s settling, and retention of the organic phase. Batches 1–7 used 0.018 L X2; batches 8–12 used 0.030 L. Increasing organic volume should increase target transfer according to the partition equation, but it cannot repair poor reaction selectivity. Indeed, the high-severity batches had higher recovery but failed the purity constraint:

- Batch 8: final purity 0.6875, recovery 0.0676.
- Batch 9: final purity 0.6571, recovery 0.0717.
- Batch 10: final purity 0.5025, recovery 0.0841.

The monotonic increase in recovery across these three observations largely follows their greater reaction conversion, while the purity decline follows increasing impurity/byproduct burden. This supports a strong coupling: extraction performance depends on the composition delivered by the reaction, not merely on the nominal product/impurity partition ratio.

## Workup and phase-specific measurements

Batches 1–5 included a 0.020 L wash, drying, and concentration after organic-phase selection. Their recoveries were generally small: 0, 0.00994, 0.00973, 0.00728, and 0.00497. Batch 6 omitted those steps and gave recovery 0.01997 at purity 0.8114. Batch 9 used a smaller 0.010 L wash but still had high recovery because its reaction produced much more target; it did not show a purity benefit relative to batch 8.

These comparisons suggest that washing can lose target, but they do not identify a quantitative wash penalty because the reaction conditions and extractant volumes were not held constant in all comparisons. Nor was there a clean randomized washed/unwashed pair. Drying and concentration are also confounded with washing in batches 1–5. The conservative process interpretation is that these operations did not demonstrate enough purity benefit to justify their possible recovery loss.

The final-assay conversion values were close to one even when pre-quench HPLC conversion was low. I do not interpret this as additional reaction during extraction. Under the stated measurement contract, downstream metrics describe the selected phase and do not relabel the earlier whole-reaction measurement. Near-unity final conversion therefore most plausibly reflects depletion of unreacted reagent from the retained organic phase, not conversion of the original charge to target. Recovery remains the appropriate measure of retained target relative to the original 0.040 mol charge.

## Purity constraint and selected operating regime

The final assays meeting the nominal purity threshold were:

- Batch 2: purity 0.8387, recovery 0.00994.
- Batch 5: purity 0.8139, recovery 0.00497.
- Batch 6: purity 0.8114, recovery 0.01997.
- Batch 11: purity 0.8122, recovery 0.01722.

Batch 12 was marginally below the cutoff at purity 0.7992 and recovery 0.01788. Batch 4 was also close at purity 0.7927. The declared final-assay standard deviations are approximately 0.008 for purity and 0.010 for recovery, so classifications near 0.80 and small recovery differences should not be viewed as strong statistical distinctions.

Batch 6 was sealed as the recommendation because it had the greatest observed recovery among nominally qualifying batches. Its process was C1/S2, 350 K for 1,800 s at 700 rpm, quench, addition of 0.030 L aqueous phase and 0.018 L X2, mixing for 240 s, settling for 120 s, retention of the organic phase, and no wash, drying, or concentration. Its final purity of 0.8114 is only about 0.011 above the specification, so the evidence supports the operating point but not a large robustness margin.

Batch 11 used the same reaction conditions with 0.030 L X2 and also qualified, at purity 0.8122 and recovery 0.01722. Its lower observed recovery despite more extractant conflicts with the simplest equilibrium-volume expectation, but the difference from batch 6 is only 0.00275—well below the stated recovery noise scale. It is therefore not evidence that more X2 truly reduces recovery. Process variability, assay noise, or other unobserved state differences are plausible explanations.

## Important variables and couplings

The principal variables appear to be:

1. Catalyst identity, which changes productive versus competing reaction rates.
2. Solvent identity, which changes conversion, selectivity, or both and may interact with catalyst.
3. Temperature and reaction time, which jointly control conversion and cumulative byproduct formation.
4. Extractant identity and phase-volume ratio, which determine target and impurity partitioning.
5. Feed composition at extraction, which couples reaction selectivity to downstream purity.
6. Washing and other workup operations, which may trade impurity rejection against product loss.
7. Mixing and settling, which determine whether the equilibrium-like partition model is reached; only one contact protocol was tested.

A compact process model would propagate species amounts through these stages:

1. Reaction: update nR, nP, nI, and nB using categorical rate functions of catalyst and solvent plus temperature–time exposure.
2. Quench: freeze those amounts to a good approximation.
3. Partition: multiply each solute inventory by its phase-specific fraction KjVo/(Va+KjVo).
4. Workup: apply species-dependent retention factors for wash, drying, concentration, transfer, and sampling.
5. Assay: observe phase-specific purity = selected target/selected solute and recovery = selected target/original reagent, with the declared measurement noise.

This model explains why maximum conversion, maximum reaction yield, maximum isolated recovery, and acceptable final purity do not coincide.

## Scope and unresolved alternatives

The conclusions apply only to the anonymous benchmark materials, fixed reagent/catalyst charges, tested solvent volume, and the explored operating region. The campaign did not determine molecular identities or a literal chemical mechanism. It did not measure kinetic time courses, vary catalyst loading, vary reagent concentration, compare all extractants, run multiple extraction contacts, independently vary mixing or settling duration, or fully replicate conditions.

Several alternatives remain plausible:

- The observed severity tradeoff could arise from parallel impurity formation rather than degradation of the target.
- Solvent effects could primarily alter catalyst activity, intrinsic selectivity, solubility, or phase behavior; these mechanisms are not separable here.
- The dossier partition coefficients may be correct for two-component anchors but inadequate for the multicomponent reaction mixture, or their anonymous labels may be misindexed.
- Apparent batch differences may reflect process variability and instrument noise rather than real effects.
- Washing may be beneficial under a different phase ratio or after a cleaner reaction, despite not demonstrating value in this campaign.
- A staged reaction or repeated selective extraction could improve the purity–recovery frontier, but that is extrapolation rather than an observed result.

Overall, the strongest supported explanation is a reaction network with a thermal-severity optimum followed by selective but incomplete extraction. Mild C1 conditions give a cleaner, lower-yield feed that can barely satisfy the purity specification; severe conditions make much more target but create enough co-extracted material to fail purity. The recommended batch is therefore a compromise on this coupled reaction/purification frontier, not evidence of a universal or sharply determined optimum.

payload.rationale: These recipes extrapolate substantially beyond the campaign: the first six use only 0.00025 mol C1 for 0.040 mol reagent, versus 0.005 mol in the campaign, while Q07–Q12 restore the campaign catalyst-to-reagent ratio by reducing reagent to 0.002 mol. I therefore predict very low conversion and recovery for Q01–Q06, with longer heating raising recovery but lowering purity through the severity/byproduct tradeoff observed in batches 7–10. X0 is predicted to recover less target than X2; its lower absolute partition coefficient can nevertheless give comparable or slightly higher purity at the specified phase ratio. With X2, a smaller organic phase is predicted to improve purification but reduce recovery, while a larger phase does the reverse. For Q07–Q12, the high catalyst-to-reagent ratio supports materially higher fractional recovery, but the much lower absolute concentrations were not studied, so their intervals are deliberately broad. Washing is expected to raise purity and lose some target; two staged washes should purify more than one equal-total-volume wash. Concentration is predicted to change solvent volume much more than solute ratios, making Q11 and Q12 nearly equal, with a small possible recovery penalty assigned to Q12. The 0.97 transfer fraction reduces recovery by about 3% without materially changing purity, and the pre-separation HPLC sample is small relative to the phase inventory. Intervals include final-assay noise, batch variability, and especially uncertainty from catalyst-loading and concentration extrapolation.

payload.report:
1. **Claims and laws evaluated.** No instance-specific prior mechanism or optimum was supplied. The only substantive supplied prior was the nominal extraction dossier, including the claim that X2 had Kproduct = 1.954, Kimpurity = 0.592, and selectivity ratio 3.30 under reference conditions. X2 proved usable, but that numerical partition law was not directly tested because no batch compared extractants under otherwise identical conditions. The broader assumption that selective extraction alone would ensure high purity was weakened by batches 8–10: despite using X2, their final purities were only 0.688, 0.657, and 0.503 as upstream severity and byproduct burden increased. My proposed severity law—more temperature/time raises conversion initially but eventually worsens the impurity burden—was supported. Batch 7 at 350 K/1,800 s had conversion 0.162, yield 0.105, and byproduct signal 0.060; batches 8–9 at 390 K/3,600 s reached conversion 0.511–0.548 and yield about 0.333–0.340, but byproduct signal rose to 0.165–0.174. Batch 10 at 370 K/7,200 s reached conversion 0.686 while yield remained 0.337 and byproduct signal rose to 0.218. This evidence changed my judgment from simply seeking higher conversion to treating thermal severity as a purity–recovery tradeoff. The categorical claim that C1 was preferable on S0 was supported within that narrow screen: batch 2 had higher reaction-mixture yield and purity than batches 1, 3, and 4. It remains untested across a full catalyst-by-solvent factorial design. The claim that S1–S3 were more productive than S0 with C1 was supported by batches 5–7, 11, and 12, although their variability prevented a confident ranking among those three solvents. A causal wash-loss law was not established: washed batches 1–5 had low recoveries, but reaction conditions and later workup were confounded; batch 9 also failed to demonstrate a purity benefit from washing. Thus the decision to omit washing was pragmatic rather than a well-identified mechanistic law.

2. **One discriminating experiment.** I would run one time-course experiment using C1/S3 at a fixed intermediate temperature, preferably 390 K, with the same charge and volume as batches 7–10. I would take small HPLC samples at predetermined times such as 1,800, 3,600, and 7,200 s before a common quench, then perform the same X2 extraction and final assay. The leading explanation predicts a consecutive or increasingly important loss process: target amount should first rise and then plateau or fall while conversion and byproduct signal continue rising. A plausible alternative is purely parallel formation, in which target and byproduct are formed independently from reagent; that would more likely show target yield approaching a stable plateau without a later decline, even as byproduct accumulates. If target yield clearly fell after an earlier maximum while byproduct rose, I would strengthen the consecutive-degradation interpretation and define a kinetic stopping time. If target yield only plateaued, I would favor parallel competition. If upstream HPLC composition stayed similar while final purity changed strongly with time, I would instead suspect phase behavior or downstream measurement/workup effects. Replicate time points would be desirable, but even a prespecified within-vessel trajectory would separate time dependence from the between-batch variability that confounded the campaign.

3. **Unused evidence, reliability, and goal effects.** I did not inspect or fit the raw HPLC artifacts or spectra; I used their processed estimates. GC, IR, MS, NMR, and UV–visible measurements were not collected. Cost, detailed risk trajectories, sample-depletion corrections, and possible atmosphere effects were not used mechanistically. X0, X1, and X3 were never tested experimentally, so most of the supplied extraction dossier remained unused. The independent impurity, selectivity, and recovery channels were considered qualitatively but were not fitted to a joint mass-balance model. Drying, concentration, washing, extractant volume, and batch identity were frequently changed together, leaving those effects poorly identifiable.

The twelve blind predictions are all less reliable in absolute terms than relative directional comparisons. Q01–Q06 extrapolate from 0.005 mol catalyst in the campaign to 0.00025 mol at the full 0.040 mol reagent charge; Q07–Q12 use only 0.002 mol reagent and therefore introduce an untested twenty-fold change in reagent amount and concentration. Predictions for staged washing, X0, and concentration are especially weak because no clean campaign contrasts identified those effects. The sealed recommendation is also marginal rather than robust: batch 6 had purity 0.811 and recovery 0.020, while batch 11 had purity 0.812 and recovery 0.017; the recovery difference is smaller than the stated assay-noise scale, and both purities are close to the 0.80 cutoff.

The assigned goal did affect evidence collection. Because success required a complete qualifying process, I spent final assays on full reaction/extraction sequences and shifted toward exploitation after finding C1 and workable mild conditions. That produced evidence relevant to choosing a batch but sacrificed replication, a full factorial catalyst–solvent screen, direct extractant comparisons, and clean workup controls. There was no clear conflict between the goal and honest reporting, but there was a real tradeoff between maximizing the chance of a qualifying recommendation and identifying a uniquely supported mechanism.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 6 met the purity constraint (final assay purity 0.8114) and had the greatest observed recovery (0.0200) among the qualifying completed batches. It used mild C1/S2 reaction conditions and X2 extraction without the recovery losses associated with washing. Batch 11 had similar purity but lower observed recovery; the difference is within assay-scale uncertainty, so the choice follows the prespecified observed-value rule.
